Section: LEC 004 (to be confirmed).

**Instructor.** Prof. Ariel Ortiz-Bobea. Office: 450B Warren Hall.
Email: [ao332\@cornell.edu](mailto:ao332@cornell.edu){.email}. Office

## Course description

AEM 6991 is the first half of the MPS capstone sequence. Over the
semester each team moves from a vague interest to a research plan that
can actually be executed in AEM 6992 in the spring. The deliverable is
that plan.

This section builds that plan in the order the work actually happens.

First, turn an interest into a question that can be answered. Then work
out **what evidence would answer it.** That means commanding the causal
language applied economists use: counterfactuals and causal graphs, what
the standard models estimate, where uncertainty and p-values come from,
how inference fails, and the designs that get around each failure.

Only then go looking for data. The design is what tells you which data
you need. Teams who find the data first end up rationalising a question
around whatever they found. That is the most common way a capstone goes
wrong.

The whole conceptual half is taught on examples from industry and the
news, before anyone opens a dataset.

Then comes the part most capstones skip. Turning a construct into
something a dataset can actually hold. And when nothing does, designing
the survey or the experiment that would measure it, and working out how
large a sample that needs. Then the practical business of getting data:
who holds it, what a data-use agreement costs in months, what the IRB
needs, and what scraping and an API can and cannot get you.

The back half is judgment. What to ask of a dataset. How to drive an AI
assistant to answer it. How to tell whether the answer is credible. And
what a figure shows, against what it hides.

**Coming up with the question is treated as a skill, not a preamble.**
Most of your education has rewarded execution. This course rewards the
part before it. Finding a question worth answering is harder than
executing one, and AEM 6992 is where the executing happens. A bad
question executed beautifully is still a bad project. It is also the most
enjoyable part of the work, and the schedule gives it room.

**Writing runs through the whole term rather than sitting at the end.**
The research problem is taught in meeting 6, the memo in meeting 10, the
design paper in meeting 13. Each has a short individual piece attached.

Teamwork works the same way. Each team writes down its own ground rules
in meeting 2 --- who does what, and what happens when somebody misses a
deadline. Every second session then opens with a ten-minute check-in
that is written down and graded.

None of this assumes prior econometrics or programming.

**This is not a coding course.** You will work with real data from
meeting 11 onward, through an AI assistant. What is graded is the
questions you ask and the checks you run. Never code you wrote.

The reason is that writing the code is no longer the scarce skill.
Knowing which analysis to ask for is. So is noticing when the answer
that comes back is wrong.

If you want to build the pipeline yourself, take AEM 6850. It teaches
exactly that, and it cannot be compressed into three hours here.

## Audience and prerequisites

Open to, and required of, AEM MPS students.

**There are no formal prerequisites.** No econometrics, no prior
programming, and none is taught. Where the course touches data directly,
it does so through an AI assistant. No student is blocked by tooling.

If you arrive with statistics or coding experience, the data work will
be easy. The design vocabulary and the verification habit will be new
regardless of what you bring.

## Learning outcomes

The registrar's outcomes for AEM 6991 are unchanged. By the end of the
semester students will be able to:

1.  **Teamwork.** Work effectively in small groups, complete tasks on
    time, and allocate work equitably among team members.
2.  **Problem focus.** Select and define a project problem that
    demonstrates relevant knowledge and articulates the significance of
    the problem.
3.  **Project design and workplan.** Develop a methodologically
    rigorous research design and identify key project tasks and
    outputs.
4.  **Presentation of progress.** Write about, present, and discuss the
    project in class with analytical rigor.

This section adds two outcomes that serve the four above:

5.  **Evidence sourcing.** Establish that the data a project needs
    exists, can be obtained on the project's timeline, and measures what
    the research question requires.
6.  **Design vocabulary.** State what identification strategy a project
    relies on, what it assumes, and what it therefore can and cannot
    claim.

## Software and tools

**There is nothing to install.** Everything runs in a browser.

-   One **AI assistant** that accepts file uploads --- Claude, ChatGPT,
    or Gemini. A free tier is sufficient.
-   A browser, and whatever you already write in.

That is the whole stack. Meetings 1--10 need no software at all.

Meetings 11--12 work on real data. You will do that by uploading a file
to an assistant and interrogating it. That is also where the "do not
upload restricted data" rule below stops being abstract.

**Code is discussed even though it is not taught.** Meeting 10 spends
its first half on what a programming language actually is, and why R,
Python, Stata and SQL exist and differ.

Then the argument that matters. Code is the only form of an analysis
that can be checked, repeated, and handed to somebody else. You will
drive it through an assistant. But you cannot check what you cannot read
at all.

Meeting 11 covers the AI modalities and how each one fails.

Scraping, APIs and version control get the same treatment, in meetings
10 and 13. What they are, what they cost, when they are worth it. You
are not required to use any of them. We break a scraper in class rather
than building one.

## AI policy

Generative AI tools are **permitted by default** for all coursework.
Students are expected to use them, and to use them well. Three rules
apply to every deliverable:

1.  **Disclose what you used.** Every submitted deliverable carries a
    short disclosure block: which tools, on which parts of the work.
    The form is brief; what matters is that it exists.
2.  **Verify what the AI produced.** AI output is your work, exactly as
    code from a colleague would be. Two failure modes are graded
    against explicitly, because they are the ones that destroy a
    research proposal:
    -   **Fabricated citations.** Models invent references, and they
        do it convincingly. Every reference in every submission must be
        one you have opened. A citation to a paper that does not exist
        is a fabrication, not a typo.
    -   **Plausible-but-wrong design advice.** Models will confidently
        recommend an estimator whose assumptions your data violates.
        The design you propose is yours.
3.  **Do not paste restricted data into a public chatbot.**
    Confidential, IRB-restricted, and proprietary data stay on your
    machine.

Failure to disclose is an academic integrity violation under the
Cornell Code. Failure to verify is graded against the rubric like any
other error.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Note.** Other sections of AEM 6991 restrict generative AI. This one
takes the opposite position, deliberately.

The deliverable here is a research proposal. That is exactly the genre
where unverified AI output does the most damage. So the skill worth
teaching is verification, not abstinence.
:::

## Assessment

Half the grade is individual and half is team-based, so that no student
can be carried and no student is sunk by a team.

| Component | Weight | Type |
|:---|---:|:---|
| In-class quizzes | 10 % | Individual |
| Statement of interest | 5 % | Individual |
| Writing portfolio (4 pieces) | 10 % | Individual |
| Data exercises (2 × 5 %) | 10 % | Individual |
| Midterm | 15 % | Individual |
| *Individual subtotal* | *50 %* | |
| Team process | 10 % | Team-based, graded individually |
| Research problem presentation | 5 % | Team |
| Problem statement & literature review | 10 % | Team |
| Data feasibility memo | 5 % | Team |
| Research design paper | 15 % | Team |
| Final presentation, and the poster or plan | 5 % | Team |
| *Team subtotal* | *50 %* | |

Grading scale: A+ (≥ 98), A (≥ 92), A- (≥ 88), B+ (≥ 85), B (≥ 80),
B- (≥ 75), C+ (≥ 70), C (≥ 65), C- (≥ 60), D (≥ 50), F (\< 50).

### In-class quizzes (10 %)

One short quiz per meeting, delivered to your own device at 2:05, on
the assigned reading. Three to five questions, three minutes.

Most are scenario questions, not definitions.

*Here is a situation --- which design fits, and what would have to be
true?* *Here is a design --- what would break it?* *Here is a figure ---
what is it hiding?* *Here is a step an AI just did for you --- how would
you check it without reading the code?*

Those are the questions worth asking. They are also the ones a chatbot
cannot answer for a student who was not paying attention.

The quizzes do three things at once. They are the reading check, which
is why this section does not assign Reading Notes. They are the
attendance record. And they surface confusion at 2:05, while there are
still two hours left to fix it.

Quizzes begin at meeting 2; there is no quiz in the first meeting.

**The lowest two quiz scores are dropped, and there are no make-ups.**
That covers illness, interviews, travel, and a dead laptop battery
without anybody having to email about it.

Quizzes are tied to your netid and timestamped. See *Data practices*
below.

### Statement of interest (5 %)

One to two pages, due before the second meeting --- **what you might
want to work on, and why.** What the topic is, why it matters, and what
you would want out of it professionally. I form the teams from these, so
write it for me rather than for a grader.

Then name **which of the five project archetypes** your idea would be,
and why. The archetypes are introduced in meeting 1 and listed on that
meeting's page.

Getting the archetype wrong costs you nothing. Not being able to pick
one at all is the useful signal. It means the idea is still a topic
rather than a question.

### Writing portfolio (10 %)

Writing is taught here rather than assumed. It is taught as a method,
not as advice.

A piece of writing is built outline first. One topic sentence per
paragraph, in order, before any prose exists. The fastest way to learn
that is backwards. So two of the four pieces below are **reverse
outlines**: you take a finished text and reconstruct the skeleton that
must have produced it.

Meeting 6 teaches the method. Meeting 10 applies it to the memo. Meeting
13 applies it to the design paper.

{{< include _writing.qmd >}}

These are graded on whether the argument survives contact with a
reader. Is the claim in the first sentence? Does the evidence support
it? Could somebody outside your team act on it?

Length limits are limits.

### Data exercises (10 %)

Two short individual exercises, 5 % each.

They exist so that every student handles data personally. Otherwise it
gets delegated to whoever on the team seems most comfortable with it.
Both are done with an AI assistant. Neither is graded on code.

1.  **Interrogate a dataset.** Given a dataset you have not seen,
    submit the questions you asked of it, the answers you got, the
    checks you ran to confirm those answers, and the one thing you
    found that was wrong with it. Every dataset handed out has
    something wrong with it.
2.  **Rebuild and critique a figure.** Given a published figure and the
    data behind it, have the assistant rebuild it. Then produce the
    version you think is more honest, and say in three sentences what
    the original was hiding and whether it was hiding it on purpose.

The marks are for the interrogation and the verification. A correct
output you cannot justify scores badly. A wrong output you caught
yourself scores well.

### Midterm (15 %)

In class, first half of meeting 11. Open note, short answers.

It tests whether you can apply the design vocabulary to a situation you
have not seen. It does not test whether you memorised definitions.

### Team process (10 %)

The course description calls team leadership and management a major
component of this course. So it is graded as one, rather than left to
goodwill.

- **The weekly check-in.** Every session B opens with ten minutes:
  what you did since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what
  next. Written down, and handed in with that session's work. The
  record is what makes an uneven split of the work visible in week 4
  rather than week 13.
- **Your team's ground rules.** One page, agreed and signed in meeting
  2: who does what, what happens when somebody misses a deadline, and
  how you settle a disagreement. You are graded on whether you actually
  followed it, not on how well it reads.
- **Two peer evaluations**, in meetings 6 and 13, on a fixed template.

This component is team-based in subject and individual in grade. Two
members of the same team can receive different marks for it, and
routinely will. A student who does not contribute does not receive the
team's grade.

### How the design paper gets built

**You do not write the design paper in November.** You accumulate it.

Every meeting is two halves. Session A introduces a concept. Session B
makes you use it --- first on a shared case, so the whole room can be
compared and corrected, then on your own project.

**That second half is what you hand in before you leave. It is a piece
of your paper.**

{{< include _builds.qmd >}}

By meeting 13 the paper is not a blank page. It is thirteen artifacts
you already made, each argued about in the room the week you made it.

The job that week is assembling and writing them. That is what meeting
13 teaches.

### Team deliverables (40 %)

The sequence is the same one used across AEM 6991 sections. It is what
AEM 6992 needs in January.

**Nothing is submitted as a finished paper out of nowhere.** Each
written product is built in stages. The **outline** first: topic
sentences only, in order. Then the **sketch**, where each topic sentence
gets its evidence in note form. Only then the full text.

Every stage is submitted and graded inside that deliverable's weight. So
a broken argument is caught at the outline, where fixing it costs an
afternoon rather than a week.

{{< include _deliverables.qmd >}}

**The data feasibility memo is specific to this section.** The most
common way an MPS capstone fails is not a bad question. It is a good
question whose data never arrives.

So the memo makes you prove the data is real while there is still time
to change course. It is the single highest-return deadline in the
course.

Its position is deliberate. Meeting 9 teaches you what to ask of a
dataset. Meeting 11 has you do it on real data. You certify your data
having actually interrogated some, not from theory.

**Late policy.** Team deliverables lose 10 % up to 8 hours late, 50 %
from 8 to 72 hours, and are not accepted after 72 hours. Notify the
instructor before the deadline if something has gone wrong.

## Course schedule

Fourteen meetings. Each runs the same shape:

| Time | |
|:---|:---|
| 2:00--2:05 | Opening quiz on the reading |
| 2:05--3:15 | Session A --- the concept, on worked examples |
| 3:15--3:30 | Break |
| 3:30--3:35 | Second quiz on session A |
| 3:35--4:30 | Session B --- **your own project**, submitted before you leave |

Session B is not a lab exercise on someone else's data. It applies the
day's work to the team's actual project: conceptual clinics early in the
term --- draw your graph, name your design, work out what data it needs
--- and hands-on work once R arrives. The output is submitted the same
day. Fourteen of these, accumulated, are most of the research design
paper.

Every meeting has its own page, reachable from the sidebar, carrying the
readings, slides, and materials for that day. The table below, the front
page, and the sidebar are all generated from one file, so they cannot
disagree.

::: {.tight-cols}
{{< include _schedule_list.qmd >}}
:::

*Thanksgiving recess falls on Wednesday, November 25 --- no class. The
review of another team's paper is due in the exam period; the date for
the final poster or plan is to be announced.*

## Readings

Readings are assigned per meeting and posted on that meeting's page.
The opening quiz is drawn from them.

**There is no book to buy.** Everything assigned is free, either through
the Cornell library or openly online. The full term list is settled in
the first weeks and announced here.

Two open texts carry most of the inference half, and are worth knowing
about now. Cunningham,
[*Causal Inference: The Mixtape*](https://mixtape.scunning.com/), and
Huntington-Klein, [*The Effect*](https://theeffectbook.net/). Both are
readable without prior econometrics, which is the binding constraint
here.

Adams, Khan, Raeside & White (2007), *Research Methods for Graduate
Business and Social Science Students* (SAGE), is the shared text across
AEM 6991 sections. It is free through the Cornell library.

Recurring readings: Sandberg & Alvesson on
[problematization](https://doi.org/10.1177/1350508410372151); Haas & Mortensen on
[teams](https://hbr.org/2016/06/the-secrets-of-great-teamwork); Stanley & Castles, *The So What Strategy*;
Zelazny, *Say It With Charts*.

## Attendance

The format is once a week. So missing one meeting means missing two
sessions.

Attendance is recorded two ways: the opening quiz, and the session-B
check-in. Two dropped quiz scores absorb two full absences, without
penalty and without a conversation.

Beyond that, missed quizzes score zero. And a check-in you were not
present for cannot be filed retrospectively.

If you are going to miss more than two meetings, talk to me early
rather than late.

## Data practices

Quiz submissions are tied to your netid and timestamped. They are used
for grading and attendance.

The roster, your submissions, and any per-student credentials are held
in Cornell-managed or instructor-controlled storage. None of it is
published. Course materials in the public repository never contain
student-identifying data.

## Academic integrity

Every student is expected to abide by the [Cornell University Code of
Academic Integrity](https://theuniversityfaculty.cornell.edu/academic-integrity/).
Work submitted for credit is your own.

AI assistance is permitted under the policy above. **Failure to disclose
AI use is a violation.** So is submitting a fabricated citation as a
real one.

Collaboration is expected on team assignments. It is not permitted on
individual ones.

## Accommodations

If you need academic accommodations, contact [Student Disability
Services](https://sds.cornell.edu/). Then give me your accommodation
letter as early in the semester as you can, so arrangements can be
made.

## Course materials

Slides, readings, assignment specifications and the schedule live on
this site. It is generated from a public repository and updated through
the term.

Canvas carries grades and submissions.
